name: Rejuvenique mask

card.summary: A 1990s electric facial mask that pulses low-level current through the face, marketed as exercising facial muscles to firm skin and soften wrinkles.
card.note: FDA-cleared (510(k), 2001) for cosmetic use, which is not an efficacy finding; reviewers describe tingling to painful sensations.

quick.overview:
The Rejuvenique is a white plastic face mask with gold-plated cushions and a battery control unit that pulses electrical stimulation through the face. It was sold as exercise for the face, aiming to firm muscles for a younger, more lifted look and fewer wrinkles.

It gained fame from a 1999 infomercial featuring actress Linda Evans. The FDA cleared it in 2001 for cosmetic use through the 510(k) pathway; clearance is not verification that it works, and no controlled trials were identified.
quick.how: Users spread conductive toning gel on the cushions, wear the mask and run a roughly 15-minute cycle, about four times a week per the booklet, as described in one review. Sensations range from light tingling to a tapping or biting feeling.
quick.risks: Reviewers describe temporary red marks and, at higher intensity, discomfort. An FDA spokesperson reportedly acknowledged no assurance of effectiveness or safety, and experts quoted in coverage warned stimulation could deepen lines. Electrical stimulators are generally cautioned for people with implanted devices.

lead: The Rejuvenique is an electric facial mask created by George E. Springer and promoted in a 1999 infomercial with Linda Evans.[1] It delivers pulsed current through gel-moistened gold-plated cushions to different areas of the face, marketed as doing for the face what exercise does for the body to firm muscles and reduce wrinkles.[1][2]

The FDA record shows a 510(k) clearance dated August 8, 2001, for the Rejuvenique System, Model RJV-10, from Salton, Inc., with the indication 'for cosmetic use'.[3] Coverage has stressed that it was never FDA-approved, which is distinct from the 510(k) clearance;[1] the FDA reportedly acknowledged no assurance it was effective or safe.[1] It launched at $180.[1]

angle.text: The manufacturer claimed the pulses exercise facial muscles to lift and firm the face. Users in published reviews saw temporary redness and no lasting change.

paras: The mask has gold-plated cushions, toning gel and a control unit on a 9-volt battery; a cycle runs four times, around 15 minutes, and the booklet recommends four sessions per week.[2]

The device became known for its eerie look. One reviewer felt tingling, then a tapping 'grabbing' sensation at higher settings, temporary red marks the booklet calls 'dimpling', and saw no change in skin.[2] Others compared it to ant bites, and experts warned stimulation could create more lines.[1]

timeline.event: Infomercial with Linda Evans makes Rejuvenique widely known.[1]
